question: What happens to a suspended complaint under the Canada Labour Code once the employee has taken the required measures?
answer:
## Suspension of Complaint and Subsequent Actions

### Ending of Suspension

The Canada Labour Code outlines the process for suspending a complaint and the conditions under which the suspension ends.
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken." - CLC-241.1, Section 241.1(3)

This indicates that a suspended complaint is lifted when the individual who initiated the suspension has fulfilled the required actions outlined in the notification provided by the Board. This signifies that the conditions that led to the suspension have been met.

### Rejection of Complaint

The Canada Labour Code also addresses the possibility of a complaint being rejected after a period of suspension.
"The Board may reject a complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), in whole or in part, (a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator; or (b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 241.1(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 241.1(2) were not taken within the specified period." - CLC-241.1, Section 241.2

This passage explains that a complaint can be rejected if the measures required during the suspension period were not completed within the specified timeframe. This suggests that the suspension is not indefinite and is tied to the individual's actions. 

### Additional Considerations

It is important to note that the Board has the discretion to suspend a complaint if it deems necessary, and the individual must take specific measures to lift the suspension. The specific measures required are outlined in the notification provided by the Board.

question: How does the Canada Labour Code protect an employee's right to receive wages from their employer in the context of other legal provisions?
answer:
## Protection of Employee's Right to Receive Wages Under Other Legal Provisions

### Section 131 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 131 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the relationship between the Canada Labour Code and other statutes concerning employee compensation. It explicitly states:
"Section 131 The fact that an employer or employee has complied with or failed to comply with any of the provisions of this Part may not be construed as affecting any right of an employee to compensation under any statute relating to compensation for employment injury or illness, or as affecting any liability or obligation of any employer or employee under any such statute."

This section is crucial because it clarifies that compliance or non-compliance with the Canada Labour Code's provisions regarding strikes and lockouts does not impact an employee's right to receive compensation under other laws.  The quote
"The fact that an employer or employee has complied with or failed to comply with any of the provisions of this Part may not be construed as affecting any right of an employee to compensation under any statute relating to compensation for employment injury or illness..." directly supports this. This means that even if an employee is involved in a strike or lockout situation, their entitlement to compensation for work-related injuries or illnesses under other applicable statutes remains unaffected.

### Section 146.5 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 146.5 focuses on the right to wages for employees participating in proceedings before the Board. It states:
"Section 146.5 An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This section ensures that employees who participate in legal proceedings related to labour matters are not financially penalized for their involvement. The quote
"...is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." clearly demonstrates the protection afforded to employees in this context. This provision guarantees that employees do not lose wages due to their participation in legal processes related to their employment.

### Labour Standards Legislation in Provinces and Territories

The Labour Reports document highlights how provincial and territorial labour standards legislation provides broad protections to employees, even those who are not traditional employees. It states:
"Act respecting  labour standards Definition “Employee” means a person who works for an employer and who is entitled to a wage..."

This indicates that provincial and territorial laws often define "employee" broadly, ensuring that a wide range of workers are covered by labour standards legislation, including those who might otherwise be classified as independent contractors. The quote
"...means a person who works for an employer and who is entitled to a wage..." directly illustrates this broad definition. This means that even if an employee's work arrangement falls outside the scope of the Canada Labour Code, they are still protected by provincial and territorial labour standards legislation regarding wages.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code, alongside provincial and territorial labour standards legislation, provides multiple layers of protection for employees' right to receive wages. Section 131 ensures that involvement in strikes or lockouts does not affect compensation rights, Section 146.5 guarantees wages for participation in legal proceedings, and provincial/territorial laws offer broad wage protections for a wide range of workers.

question: Are there any exceptions to the typical rules governing when a trade union can apply for certification, particularly when a collective agreement is in place?
answer:
## Exceptions to Certification Application Rules

### Application for Certification: Exception (CLC-24.1)

Section 24.1 of the Canada Labour Code outlines an exception to the typical rules governing when a trade union can apply for certification, even when a collective agreement is already in place.
"A trade union that is not certified but has entered into a collective agreement the term of which has not expired may, despite paragraphs 24(2)(c) and (d), make an application for certification at any time, in respect of the unit to which the collective agreement applies or substantially the same unit."

This indicates that even if a collective agreement exists, preventing applications for a certain period, a union can still apply for certification *as long as the collective agreement is still valid*. This exception allows a union to seek certification even when the usual time restrictions apply, provided the collective agreement is still in effect. This is a significant exception to the standard rules, offering a pathway for unions to gain certification even when a collective agreement is already in place.



### Application for Certification: Limitation (CLC-24)

While not a direct exception, Section 24(2) outlines limitations on when a union can apply for certification, particularly when a collective agreement is in force.
"(c) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation; and (d) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation."

This section specifies that a union cannot apply for certification during the term of a collective agreement, with specific timeframes outlined based on the agreement's duration. This implies that the application must occur *after* the collective agreement has expired or is nearing its expiration.



### Application for Certification: Where certification prohibited (CLC-25)

Section 25 addresses situations where certification is prohibited, which indirectly relates to the timing of applications.
"Notwithstanding anything in this Part, where the Board is satisfied that a trade union is so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired, the Board shall not certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for any unit comprised of employees of the employer and any collective agreement between the trade union and the employer that applies to any such employees shall be deemed not to be a collective agreement for the purposes of this Part."

This section states that if a union is deemed to be dominated or influenced by an employer, certification will be denied. This means that even if a collective agreement is in place, the union cannot be certified if it is not truly independent and acting in the best interests of the employees.



### Application for Certification: Excetion (CLC-24.1)

As mentioned above, Section 24.1 provides an exception to the typical rules, allowing a union to apply for certification even if a collective agreement is in place, as long as the agreement has not expired. This is a key exception that allows unions to seek certification even when the usual time restrictions apply.

question: Can an employer take disciplinary action against an employee who has exercised their rights under the Canada Labour Code, and if so, under what circumstances?
answer:
## Employer Disciplinary Action and Employee Rights under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 147: General Prohibition on Disciplinary Action

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general prohibition against employers taking disciplinary action against employees for exercising their rights under the Code.
"...or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

This section explicitly states that an employer cannot take disciplinary action against an employee
"...has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part." This means that an employer cannot retaliate against an employee for exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code.

### Section 147.1: Abuse of Rights

However, Section 147.1 provides an exception to this general prohibition. It allows an employer to take disciplinary action against an employee who has "willfully abused" their rights under sections 128 and 129.
"An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights."

This means that if an employee knowingly and intentionally misused their rights under the Code, the employer may be able to take disciplinary action. The employer has the burden of demonstrating that the employee willfully abused their rights.

### Summary

In summary, an employer generally cannot take disciplinary action against an employee for exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code, as outlined in Section 147. However, this protection does not apply if the employee has willfully abused their rights, in which case the employer may be able to take disciplinary action under Section 147.1.

question: How can the Governor in Council regulate the operation and procedures of workplace committees?
answer:
## Governor in Council Regulation of Workplace Committees

The Canada Labour Code outlines several ways in which the Governor in Council (GIC) can regulate the operation and procedures of workplace committees. These regulations are primarily enacted through the authority granted to the GIC within the Canada Labour Code itself.

### Authority for Regulation

Section 135.1 states that
"Subject to this section, a policy committee or a work place committee shall consist of at least two chairpersons selected from among the committee members." (no source found for the quotation) This indicates that the Code establishes the basic framework for workplace committees, but allows for further regulation.

### Specific Areas of Regulation

The Code allows the GIC to regulate various aspects of workplace committee operation and procedures. 

*   **Rules of Procedure:
"Subject to subsections 134.1(7) and 135(10) and any regulations made under subsection 135.2(1), a committee shall establish its own rules of procedure in respect of the terms of office, not exceeding two years, of its members and the time, place and frequency of regular meetings of the committee and may establish any rules of procedure for its operation that it considers advisable." This indicates that the GIC can set parameters for the rules of procedure that committees must follow.
*   **Staffing:
"The judge may engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the judge in conducting the inquiry, establish the terms and conditions of their engagement and, with the approval of the Treasury Board, fix and pay their remuneration and expenses." This suggests that the GIC can regulate the staffing of inquiries conducted under section 12.08.
*   **Disciplinary Measures:** Section 12.14 outlines the process for disciplinary measures against members of inquiries. It states that
"The judge may, in the report, recommend that the member be suspended without pay or removed from office or that any other disciplinary measure or any remedial measure be taken if, in the opinion of the judge, the member (a) has become incapacitated from the proper execution of that office by reason of infirmity; (b) has been guilty of misconduct; (c) has failed in the proper execution of that office; or (d) has been placed, by conduct or otherwise, in a position that is incompatible with the due execution of that office." This implies that the GIC can regulate the disciplinary measures that can be taken against members of inquiries.

In summary, the Governor in Council's regulatory power extends to defining the structure, rules of operation, staffing, and disciplinary procedures of workplace committees and inquiries, ensuring a framework for their effective and fair functioning.

Marginal note: Change of activity or sale of a provincial business (3) Where, as a result of a change of activity, a provincial business becomes subject to this Part, or such a business is sold to an employer who is subject to this Part, (a) the trade union that, pursuant to the laws of the province, is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the provincial business continues to be their bargaining agent for the purposes of this Part; (b) a collective agreement that applied to employees employed in the provincial business at the time of the change or sale continues to apply to them and is binding on the employer or on the person to whom the business is sold; (c) any proceeding that at the time of the change or sale was before the labour relations board or other person or authority that, under the laws of the province, is competent to decide the matter, continues as a proceeding under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party; and (d) any grievance that at the time of the change or sale was before an arbitrator or arbitration board continues to be processed under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party. question: How do changes in business activities or ownership affect the continuity of labour relations, collective agreements, and dispute resolution processes under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Impact of Business Changes on Labour Relations under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 44: Definitions of "Business" and "Sale of Business"

Section 44(1) defines "business" broadly to include
"...any federal work, undertaking or business and any part thereof..." This broad definition is crucial because it establishes the scope of the Labour Code's application. It also defines "sell" to include
"...the transfer or other disposition of the business and, for the purposes of this definition, leasing a business is deemed to be selling it." This is important because it clarifies that a change in ownership or control, even through leasing, triggers the provisions of this section.

### Section 44: Continuity of Trade Union Representation After a Sale

Section 44(2)(a) addresses the continuity of trade union representation when a business is sold. It states,
"...a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent..." This means that the trade union representing the employees remains the same even after the business is sold. This provision ensures that the employees continue to have representation from the same union they had before the change in ownership.

### Section 44: Binding Nature of Existing Collective Agreements

Section 44(2)(c) is particularly important for the continuity of collective agreements. It states,
"...the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business..." This means that the new owner of the business is obligated to honor the existing collective agreement. This provision protects the terms and conditions of employment that were negotiated with the previous employer.

### Section 44: Continuation of Pending Disputes

Section 44(2)(d) ensures that ongoing labour disputes are not disrupted by a change in ownership. It states,
"...any proceeding that at the time of the change or sale was before the labour relations board or other person or authority that, under the laws of the province, is competent to decide the matter, continues as a proceeding under this Part, with such modifications as the circumstances require and, where applicable, with the person to whom the provincial business is sold as a party..." This ensures that grievances and other legal proceedings are able to continue under the Labour Code framework, even after the business has been sold.

### Section 44: Impact on Provincial Businesses

Section 44(3) specifically addresses the impact of changes affecting provincial businesses. It states that if a provincial business becomes subject to the Labour Code as a result of a change in activity or is sold to an employer subject to the Labour Code, the trade union representing the employees continues to be their bargaining agent. It also ensures that existing collective agreements remain in force and that ongoing legal proceedings continue under the Labour Code. This provision ensures that the rights of employees in provincial businesses are protected during periods of change.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code, through Section 44, provides a framework for ensuring the continuity of labour relations, collective agreements, and dispute resolution processes when there are changes in business activities or ownership. It protects the rights of employees by ensuring that they retain their existing union representation, that existing collective agreements remain in force, and that ongoing disputes can continue to be resolved under the Labour Code.

If 1 of the other general holidays, not listed directly above, falls on a non-work day, then a holiday with pay may be added to your annual vacation. It can also be granted as a general holiday with pay at a time convenient to both you and your employer.  **Substituting a general holiday for another day** An employer may substitute a general holiday for another day for 1 or more employees. If you are an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, there must be a written agreement on the substitution between the:  employer union, and employee(s)  If you are an employee who is not subject to a collective agreement, the substitution must be approved by:  you, in writing, if the substitution applies to you only, or at least 70% of the affected employees, if it applies to multiple employees. The employer must post the notice of substitution for at least 30 days before it takes effect  You may also request to substitute a general holiday with another day as part of your request for flexible work arrangements. This request must be authorized by your employer in writing.  **Calculating general holiday pay** Your general holiday pay is calculated based on how your wages are calculated. For most employees, general holiday pay is equal to at least one-twentieth (1/20th) of the wages, excluding overtime pay, earned in the 4-week period immediately before the week in which the general holiday occurs. A general holiday pay calculator is available to estimate general holiday entitlement and pay.  Note: The general holiday pay calculator should not be used to calculate entitlements and pay if you are employed in a multi-employer establishment, such as longshoring."

question: How are alternative holidays with pay typically arranged for employees when a general holiday falls on a non-working day, and what factors influence the scheduling of these alternative holidays?
answer:
## Alternative Holiday Arrangements for Non-Working General Holidays

### General Principle of Alternative Holiday
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code establishes the fundamental principle that employees are entitled to an alternative holiday with pay when a general holiday falls on a day they would otherwise not be working. The key is that the holiday must be granted "at some other time," providing flexibility in scheduling.

### Factors Influencing Scheduling

The scheduling of these alternative holidays is influenced by several factors, as outlined in the workplace information.

**Flexibility for Employee and Employer:
"...by adding it to their annual vacation or by granting it at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer..."

The law emphasizes flexibility, allowing for the holiday to be added to the employee's annual vacation or scheduled at a mutually agreeable time. This acknowledges the diverse needs of both the employee and the employer.

**Specific Holiday Scenarios:
"...when New Year’s Day, Canada Day, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Remembrance Day, Christmas Day or Boxing Day falls on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay on the working day immediately preceding or following the general holiday."

This provides a specific rule for certain holidays that often fall on weekends, ensuring the employee receives the holiday pay on a day that is part of their regular work schedule.

**Collective Agreements:
"...subject to a collective agreement, there must be a written agreement on the substitution between the:  employer union, and employee(s)..."

When an employee is covered by a collective agreement, the terms of that agreement dictate the arrangement for alternative holidays. A written agreement is required to specify how these holidays will be handled.

**Individual Agreements:
"If you are an employee who is not subject to a collective agreement, the substitution must be approved by:  you, in writing, if the substitution applies to you only, or at least 70% of the affected employees, if it applies to multiple employees."

For employees without a collective agreement, the arrangement requires either individual agreement or approval from a significant portion of the affected employees.

**Employer Notification:
"The employer must post the notice of substitution for at least 30 days before it takes effect..."

To ensure transparency and allow employees to plan accordingly, employers are required to provide advance notice of any changes to the standard holiday arrangements.

In summary, the arrangement of alternative holidays with pay when a general holiday falls on a non-working day is designed to be flexible, allowing for scheduling at a mutually convenient time. However, the specific details of this arrangement can be influenced by collective agreements, individual agreements, and employer notification procedures.

question: What are the consequences for a complainant if the Board decides to suspend or reject their complaint under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Suspension of Complaint

### Consequences of Suspension

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific consequences for a complainant if the Board decides to suspend consideration of their complaint.
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

This indicates that the Board, or "Head" in this context, has the authority to suspend the review of a complaint. The complainant is required to take certain measures before the suspension ends.
"If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures."

This highlights that the complainant will receive written notification detailing the required actions and the timeframe for completing them.
"The suspension ends when, in the Head’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

The suspension is lifted once the complainant fulfills the specified requirements within the given timeframe.

## Rejection of Complaint

The Canada Labour Code also details the consequences of the Board rejecting a complaint.
"The Board may reject a complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), in whole or in part, (a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator; or (b) if consideration of the complaint was suspended under subsection 241.1(1) and if, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice under subsection 241.1(2) were not taken within the specified period."

If a complaint is rejected, the complainant will receive written notification with the reasons for the rejection. The reasons for rejection can include the complaint falling outside the Board's jurisdiction, being frivolous, vexatious, or not made in good faith, or if the matter has already been adequately addressed through other legal avenues.
"If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the complainant in writing, with..."

It is important to note that a rejection can occur if the complainant fails to take the required measures following a suspension of the complaint.

question: What are the requirements for a conciliation board to proceed with a sitting when one of its members is absent?
answer:
## Conciliation Board Sittings with Absent Members

### Section 85(2) - Quorum and Absence
"...in the absence of any member, the other members shall not proceed unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the requirements for a conciliation board to proceed with a sitting when a member is absent. It explicitly states that the board cannot conduct business if a member is absent without having been given "reasonable notice" of the sitting. This ensures fairness and allows the absent member to be present, if possible, to participate in the proceedings. The requirement for "reasonable notice" implies a practical consideration for the member's ability to attend, taking into account factors such as distance and scheduling conflicts.

question: Who has the authority to appoint a member to a joint planning committee if there is a vacancy due to the failure of a trade union or redundant employees to make an appointment?
answer:
## Authority to Appoint in Case of Vacancy

### Section 217: Head's Appointment in Lieu of Failure
"If a trade union fails, or redundant employees fail, to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as provided in sections 214 and 215, the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees, as the case may be, and that member is a representative of the redundant employees represented by the trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint the member, as the case may be."

This section of the Canada Labour Code explicitly outlines the authority to appoint a member when a vacancy occurs due to the failure of a trade union or redundant employees to make an appointment. 

The key takeaway is that "the Head" has the power to appoint a member
"...in lieu of that trade union or those employees..." This appointment is made "on application of any redundant employee," suggesting that the right to seek this appointment rests with the redundant employees themselves. 

Furthermore, the appointed member is designated as a representative of either the redundant employees represented by the failing trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint a representative. This ensures that the appointed member effectively fills the gap and continues to represent the interests of the redundant employees.

question: What are the specific timelines and processes that a trade union or a corporation/business must follow when applying for certification or an order related to collective agreements or arbitral awards after a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes part of a corporation or business?
answer:
## Section 47: Timelines and Processes for Trade Unions and Corporations/Businesses After Federal Public Administration Changes

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the specific timelines and processes involved when a portion of the federal public administration transitions into a corporation or business. It addresses both trade union certification and orders related to collective agreements or arbitration awards.

### Timeline for Collective Agreement/Arbitration Award Continuation
"Where the name of any portion of the federal public administration specified from time to time in Schedule I, IV or V to the Financial Administration Act is deleted and that portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which this Part applies, or where a portion of the federal public administration included in another portion of the federal public administration specified in those Schedules is severed from the portion in which it was included and established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business, (a) a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This passage establishes that existing collective agreements or arbitration awards remain in effect. The key timeline here is the duration until the agreement's term expires. However, the continuation is subject to further processes outlined in subsections (3) to (7).

### Application for Order - 120th to 150th Day Window
"...the corporation or business, as employer of the employees, or any bargaining agent affected by the change in employment, may, during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date on which the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of the corporation or business, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters referred to in subsection (4)."

This specifies a 30-day window, from the 120th to the 150th day after the transition, during which the corporation or business or a bargaining agent can apply to the Board for an order. This application is for the Board to determine whether the employees constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and which union should be the bargaining agent for each unit.

### Application for Order - 151st to 210th Day Window
"Where no application for an order is made pursuant to subsection (3) within the period specified in that subsection, the corporation or business, as employer of the employees, or any bargaining agent bound by a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by subsection (1), is continued in force, may, during the period commencing on the one hundred and fifty-first day and ending on the two hundred and tenth day after the date the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of the corporation or business, apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the other party a notice to bargain collectively."

If no order is sought within the initial 30-day window, a second 60-day window opens, from the 151st to the 210th day. During this period, the corporation or business or a bargaining agent can apply for an order granting leave to serve a notice to bargain collectively.

### Application for Leave to Serve a Notice to Bargain Collectively
"Where the Board determines, pursuant to paragraph (4)(c), that a collective agreement or arbitral award shall remain in force, either party to the collective agreement or arbitral award may, not later than sixty days after the date the Board makes its determination, apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the other party a notice to bargain collectively."

This passage details the process for obtaining permission to serve a notice to bargain collectively. It states that either party to the collective agreement or arbitration award can apply for leave within 60 days of the Board's determination regarding the agreement's continuation.

### Notice to Bargain Collectively
"Where the Board determines, pursuant to paragraph (4)(c), that a collective agreement or arbitral award shall remain in force, either party to the collective agreement or arbitral award may, not later than sixty days after the date the Board makes its determination, apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the other party a notice to bargain collectively."

This section specifies that after the Board determines that a collective agreement or arbitration award will remain in force, either party can apply for an order granting leave to serve a notice to bargain collectively.

In summary, the timeline and processes are as follows:

1.  **Initial Period (120th-150th day):** Corporation/business or bargaining agent can apply for an order determining bargaining units and bargaining agents.
2.  **If no order is sought (151st-210th day):** Corporation/business or bargaining agent can apply for an order granting leave to serve a notice to bargain collectively.
3.  **After Board determination of agreement continuation:** Either party to the agreement can apply for an order granting leave to serve a notice to bargain collectively within 60 days.

question: Can the Board's determination of a question regarding a business sale or change in business activity be considered final and binding?
answer:
## Analysis of Board Determination on Business Sale/Change of Activity

### Section 45: Board's Authority to Determine Bargaining Units
"Section 45 In the case of a sale or change of activity referred to in section 44, the Board may, on application by the employer or any trade union affected, determine whether the employees affected constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining."

This section establishes the Board's power to determine bargaining units following a business sale or change in activity. It explicitly states that the Board *may* determine whether the affected employees should be grouped into one or more bargaining units. This indicates a significant role for the Board in addressing the organizational implications of such transactions.

### Section 46: Board's Obligation to Determine Questions Arising from Business Transactions
"Section 46 The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business."

This section is crucial to answering the question. It clearly states that
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business..." This implies that the Board's determination on these specific questions is not merely discretionary but is an *obligation*.

### Section 156: Finality of Board Orders and Decisions
"Section 156 (1) Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Part."

These sections establish the finality of the Board's orders and decisions. Specifically, Section 156(1) states that
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." This means that the Board's determination regarding a business sale or change in activity, as outlined in sections 45 and 46, is final and binding and cannot be challenged in court.

**Conclusion:**

Based on the provided text, the Board's determination of a question regarding a business sale or change in business activity *is* considered final and binding. Section 46 mandates the Board to determine such questions, and Section 156 ensures that any resulting order or decision is final and not subject to judicial review. Therefore, the Board's determination carries significant weight and is not easily overturned.

question: How do leaves of absence under Division VII or VIII, or certain specified absences, affect an employee's vacation plans according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Impact of Leaves of Absence on Vacation Plans

### Section 187.1: Interrupting Vacation for Leaves of Absence

Section 187.1 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the situation where an employee interrupts a vacation to take a leave of absence. It states:
"An employee may interrupt a vacation granted to them under this Division in order to permit them to take a leave of absence under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5 or to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1)."

This section explicitly permits employees to interrupt their vacation for specific reasons, including leaves of absence under Division VII or VIII, which are related to reservist duties. This indicates that the interruption of a vacation is permissible and does not necessarily forfeit the vacation time.

Furthermore, the section outlines how the interruption and subsequent resumption of vacation are treated under specific circumstances. It details that if an employee interrupts their vacation to take leave under certain sections (205.1, 206, 206.1 and 206.3 to 206.9) and resumes the vacation immediately after the leave, Section 209.1 applies to them
"...as if they did not resume the vacation before returning to work." This suggests that the interruption is treated as if it never happened for the purpose of applying certain provisions.

Similarly, if an employee interrupts their vacation to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1) and resumes the vacation immediately after the leave, subsection 239(7) applies to them
"...as if they did not resume the vacation before returning to work." This reinforces the idea that the interruption is treated as if it never happened for the purpose of applying certain provisions.

### Section 187.2: Postponing Vacation Due to Leaves of Absence

Section 187.2 further clarifies the relationship between leaves of absence and vacation by allowing employees to postpone their vacation. It states:
"Despite paragraph 185(a) or any term or condition of employment, an employee may postpone their vacation until after the day on which a leave of absence taken under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5, or an absence due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1), ends."

This section explicitly states that an employee can postpone their vacation until *after* the leave of absence ends. This means that the leave of absence effectively extends the vacation period, allowing the employee to enjoy their vacation at a later time.

The section also requires the employee to provide the employer with prior written notice of the postponement. This ensures that the employer is aware of the change in plans and can make necessary adjustments.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code provides mechanisms for employees to interrupt or postpone their vacation plans due to leaves of absence under Division VII or VIII, or certain specified absences. These provisions aim to balance the employee's right to take leave with their entitlement to vacation time.

question: What is the general purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under this section of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Purpose of Regulations under Canada Labour Code Section 111

### Administrative and Procedural Matters

Section 111 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to make regulations concerning a wide range of administrative and procedural matters. This includes defining how notices, requests, and reports are to be handled.
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) prescribing to or by whom and in what manner any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received..."

This indicates that the regulations can establish the protocols for communication between the Minister and various parties, ensuring proper and efficient information flow.

### Forms and Content of Communications

The regulations also cover the specific forms and content of various communications required under the Code. This encompasses notices related to collective bargaining, conciliation, and dispute resolution.
"(d) prescribing the form and content of a notice to commence collective bargaining; (e) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 71 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice; (f) prescribing the form and content of a notice under section 87.2 and prescribing any additional information that is to be furnished with such a notice..."

These provisions highlight the ability to standardize communication, ensuring clarity and completeness in important labor-related notifications.

### Procedural Aspects of Dispute Resolution

Furthermore, the regulations address procedural aspects related to dispute resolution processes, including time limits, jurisdictional rules, and the handling of decisions and orders.
"(g) prescribing a time limit for the purposes of subsection 99.01(1), as well as rules respecting the Board’s jurisdiction, and the validity of a decision or order made by it, after the time limit..."

This demonstrates the power to establish the framework for ensuring timely and legally sound dispute resolution.

### Public Access to Information

The regulations also extend to public access to information, specifically concerning copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister.
"...prescribing the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister; (k) prescribing the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof..."

This indicates a provision for transparency and public accountability in labor-related decisions.

In essence, the regulations under Section 111 serve to provide the detailed rules and procedures necessary for the effective administration and implementation of the Canada Labour Code. They cover a broad spectrum of administrative, procedural, and informational aspects, ensuring clarity, consistency, and efficiency in labor relations.

question: How does the Board ensure that its orders remain relevant and effective in changing circumstances?
answer:
## Review and Amendment of Orders

### Section 18 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 18 outlines the Board's power to adapt its orders to evolving circumstances. It states:
"The Board may review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it, and may rehear any application before making an order in respect of the application."

This indicates a proactive approach to ensuring relevance. The Board isn't bound by its initial decisions; it has the authority to revisit and modify orders as needed. This flexibility is crucial for maintaining effectiveness in a dynamic environment. The ability to "review, rescind, amend, alter or vary" an order allows the Board to respond to unforeseen changes in the law, industry practices, or other relevant factors. Furthermore, the Board can "rehear any application" before making a new order, ensuring that the revised order is informed by the most current information and perspectives.

## Appeals and Order Modification

### Section 251.12 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 251.12 addresses the process of appeals and how the Board can ensure its orders remain relevant during this process. It states:
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..."

This demonstrates that the Board can proactively adjust its orders even during the appeal process. The Board has the power to "confirm, rescind or vary" the decision being appealed, ensuring that the order remains relevant and effective regardless of the outcome of the appeal. This power is essential for maintaining the integrity of the Board's decisions and ensuring that they continue to serve their intended purpose.

### Section 22 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 22 reinforces the finality of Board orders and decisions, but also includes a provision regarding the Board's standing to address the standard of review. It states:
"The Board has standing to appear in proceedings referred to in subsection (1) for the purpose of making submissions regarding the standard of review to be used with respect to decisions of the Board and the Board’s jurisdiction, policies and procedures."

This suggests that the Board is actively involved in shaping the framework for reviewing its own decisions. By having the standing to make submissions regarding the standard of review, the Board can ensure that its orders are consistently interpreted and applied in a way that reflects current legal and policy considerations. This proactive engagement in the review process helps to maintain the relevance and effectiveness of the Board's orders over time.

## Finality and No Review

### Section 22 and Section 156 of the Canada Labour Code

Both Section 22 and Section 156 state that
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

While this emphasizes the finality of Board orders, it also implies a mechanism for ensuring relevance. The finality of the order necessitates that the Board has carefully considered all relevant factors and has made a well-reasoned decision. This careful consideration, coupled with the Board's ability to review and amend orders as needed, ensures that the orders remain relevant and effective in changing circumstances. The finality also provides stability and predictability for the parties involved, while still allowing for necessary adjustments through the review and amendment process.

question: What is the purpose of establishing a joint planning committee and when must an employer take this step after notifying the Head under section 212?
answer:
## Purpose of Establishing a Joint Planning Committee

The purpose of establishing a joint planning committee is to facilitate cooperation between the employer and redundant employees in developing an adjustment program. Section 214(1) states:
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217." This indicates that the committee's primary function is to work collaboratively on a plan to mitigate the negative impacts of group termination.

## Timing of Establishment

An employer must establish the joint planning committee "as soon as possible after giving the notice" to the Head under section 212. Section 216 reinforces this requirement, stating that the committee
"...must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212." This means the employer has a limited timeframe of two weeks following the initial notification to initiate the committee's formation and begin its work.

## Composition of the Committee

Section 214(3) specifies the composition of the joint planning committee:
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer." This ensures that both the employees and the employer have a voice in the planning process, promoting a balanced and mutually acceptable adjustment program.

question: What are the implications and prerequisites for filing an order of the Board in the Federal Court?
answer:
## Filing an Order of the Board in the Federal Court

### Section 23: Filing Requirement and Conditions

Section 23(1) of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process for filing a Board order or decision in the Federal Court. It states that
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose."

This indicates that the primary prerequisite for filing an order in the Federal Court is a written request from any individual or organization impacted by the order or decision. The Board has discretion to refuse filing if it believes there is no risk of non-compliance with the order or if filing would be unnecessary.

### Section 23: Process and Acceptance

Section 23(2) details the procedure when the Board decides to file an order. It specifies that the Board must
"...specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding." This means that a simple written notification to the court is sufficient for the order to be officially filed and registered.

### Section 23: Legal Effect of Registration

Section 23(3) clarifies the legal implications of a registered order or decision. It states that
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court."

This is a significant implication, as a registered order in the Federal Court carries the same legal weight as a judgment from that court. This allows for enforcement of the order through the Federal Court system, providing a mechanism for ensuring compliance.

### Section 23.1: Filing in Provincial Superior Court

Section 23.1 provides an alternative to filing in the Federal Court. It states that
"The Board may, on application by a person or organization affected by an order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the superior court of a province. Section 23 applies, with any modifications that the circumstances require, to an order or decision filed in such a superior court."

This indicates that the Board has the option to file in a provincial superior court, and the procedures outlined in Section 23 apply accordingly. This provision offers flexibility depending on the specific circumstances and the location of the affected parties.

In summary, the prerequisites for filing a Board order in the Federal Court include a written request from an affected party. The process involves a written notification to the court, and the registered order carries the force of a judgment, allowing for enforcement through the Federal Court system. The Board also has the option to file in a provincial superior court.

question: What happens to the Minister's powers of appointment under the Act when they are delegated to another person?
answer:
## Delegation of Ministerial Powers

### Section 140: General Delegation
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Minister may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers, duties or functions the Minister is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

This section establishes the fundamental principle of delegation. It states that the Minister has the authority to delegate their powers, duties, and functions to other individuals or groups, provided that the delegation is subject to any terms and conditions set by the Minister. This means the Minister retains the power to define the scope and limitations of the delegation.

### Section 140.1: Delegation by the Head
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform for the purposes of this Part. The Head may make the delegation subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."

This subsection clarifies that the "Head" (likely referring to the head of the relevant department or agency) also has the power to delegate. It mirrors the language of Section 140, emphasizing the importance of terms and conditions and the Head's discretion in setting those conditions.

### Section 140.2: Agreements with Provinces
"Subject to subsection (3), the Minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with any province or any provincial body specifying the terms and conditions under which the Minister may delegate to a person employed by that province or provincial body the powers, duties or functions that the Minister or the Head is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

This section outlines a specific mechanism for delegation – through agreements with provinces. It allows the Minister (or the Head, implicitly) to delegate powers to individuals employed by a province or provincial body, provided that the Governor in Council approves the agreement. This demonstrates a collaborative approach to delegation, enabling the transfer of responsibilities to provincial entities.

### Section 140.5: Liability of Delegated Persons
"A person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the actual or purported exercise of those powers or performance of those duties or functions."

This section addresses the liability of individuals who receive delegated powers. It provides protection against personal liability for actions taken in good faith while exercising those delegated powers. This encourages delegation by mitigating the risk of personal responsibility for errors or omissions.

In summary, the Minister's powers of appointment can be delegated to qualified individuals or groups, subject to terms and conditions set by the Minister or the Head. This delegation can also occur through agreements with provinces, enabling the transfer of responsibilities to provincial entities. Furthermore, those who receive delegated powers are protected from personal liability for actions taken in good faith.

question: What is the legislative intent behind the provision regarding proceedings under this Part of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Legislative Intent Behind Proceedings Under the Canada Labour Code (CLC) Part

The legislative intent behind the provisions regarding proceedings under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (CLC) appears to be multifaceted, focusing on establishing a clear framework for addressing workplace complaints, ensuring timely resolution, and protecting the rights of employees and employers. The various sections highlight a concern for fairness, efficiency, and procedural safeguards.

### Limitation Period and Timeliness

Section 257(2) establishes a "limitation period" for initiating proceedings. This indicates a legislative intent to ensure that complaints are brought within a reasonable timeframe. The provision states:
"Proceedings in respect of an offence under this Part may be instituted at any time within but not later than three years after the time when the subject-matter of the proceedings arose." This aims to prevent stale claims and promote timely resolution of workplace issues. The three-year limit provides a balance between allowing sufficient time for investigation and ensuring that matters are addressed promptly.

### Procedural Safeguards and Fairness

Section 257(3) specifically addresses the requirement for "Minister’s consent" before initiating proceedings against a director of a corporation. This suggests a legislative intent to ensure that such proceedings are carefully considered and not initiated without proper justification. This provision likely aims to prevent frivolous or politically motivated actions against corporate directors.

### Employee Rights and Compensation During Proceedings

Section 146.5 outlines the rights of employees who participate in proceedings. It states:
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work." This demonstrates a legislative intent to protect employees from financial hardship while they participate in the process. The provision ensures that employees are not penalized for exercising their rights and are compensated for time spent in proceedings.

### Restrictions on Conciliation and Review

Section 86 prohibits certain actions related to conciliation and proceedings. It states:
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court (a) to question the appointment of, or refusal to appoint, a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or the establishment of, or the refusal to establish, a conciliation board; or (b) to review, prohibit or restrain any proceeding of a conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board." This indicates a legislative intent to preserve the integrity of the conciliation and mediation process. By restricting court intervention in these matters, the legislation aims to encourage voluntary resolution of disputes and avoid undue interference with the work of conciliators and mediators.

### Defining Circumstances for Withdrawal of Complaints

Section CLSR-29.3 focuses on the conditions under which a complaint can be considered withdrawn. It states:
"A prescribed circumstance for the purposes of paragraph 251.01(3)(b) of the Act is the making of a complaint under subsection 251.01(1) of the Act, if a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts was previously made under that subsection in accordance with subsection 251.01(2) of the Act and that complaint was withdrawn because it is incomplete or contains an error." This suggests a legislative intent to provide a mechanism for addressing incomplete or erroneous complaints, allowing for a fresh start while acknowledging the previous attempt.

question: What is the intended effect of setting a time limit for the validity of regulations made under section 296 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Intended Effect of Time Limit on Regulations under Section 296

### Overview

Section 296 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations concerning pilot projects. A key aspect of this section is the provision regarding the validity of these regulations. The intended effect of setting a time limit for the validity of these regulations is to ensure periodic review and potential renewal of the regulations, promoting ongoing relevance and effectiveness.

### Analysis of Relevant Text

The text states:
"Previous Version Marginal note: Repeal Section 263.1 Unless they are repealed earlier, regulations made under section 263 are repealed on the fifth anniversary of the day on which they come into force. 2018, c. 27, s. 504..."

This indicates that regulations made under section 263, which is very similar to section 296, are subject to a time limit. They are repealed on the fifth anniversary of their coming into force, unless repealed earlier.

The inclusion of this time limit serves several purposes:

*   **Ensuring Regular Scrutiny:** The time limit compels the government to periodically review the regulations. This ensures that the regulations remain relevant and effective in addressing the evolving needs of pilot projects and improving employee rights.
*   **Adaptability to Changing Circumstances:**  Regulations created for pilot projects may need to be updated to reflect changes in the labour market, technological advancements, or evolving legal interpretations. A time limit allows for these adjustments.
*   **Accountability and Transparency:**  The sunset clause promotes accountability by requiring the government to justify the continued validity of the regulations. It also enhances transparency by making the regulations subject to periodic review and potential renewal.

Therefore, the time limit on regulations made under section 296 is intended to ensure that these regulations remain current, effective, and responsive to the needs of pilot projects and the protection of employee rights.

question: What happens to an employee's status under the Canada Labour Code if they cease to work due to a lockout or strike, or are dismissed contrary to the Code?
answer:
## Employee Status During Lockouts and Strikes

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific provisions regarding employee status during lockouts and strikes, particularly concerning reinstatement after such events.

### Section 87.5: Rights Unaffected and Reinstatement

Section 87.5 addresses the rights of employees during a strike or lockout. It states:
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This indicates that during a lockout or strike, an employer is restricted from unilaterally changing an employee's terms of employment. This protection extends to wages, benefits, and other conditions of employment.

Furthermore, Section 87.6 explicitly states:
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person."

This provision mandates reinstatement of employees who participated in a strike or lockout, prioritizing their return over hiring new employees. This ensures that employees are not penalized for exercising their right to strike or for being locked out by the employer.

### Section 87.4: Maintaining Services During a Strike or Lockout

Section 87.4 also provides important context. It states:
"...the supply of those services, the operation of those facilities and the production of those goods that it considers necessary to continue in order to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public..."

This section clarifies that even during a strike or lockout, employees who are assigned to maintain essential services are still considered employees of the company and are entitled to their existing terms and conditions of employment. This ensures that essential services are maintained while protecting the rights of striking or locked-out employees.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code protects employees' rights during lockouts and strikes by preventing changes to their terms of employment and mandating their reinstatement after the dispute is resolved. It also ensures that employees performing essential services during these periods retain their employment status and rights.

LABOUR-REPORTS-7_61:

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-7_61", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Anti-reprisal protection for  concerted activity** Studies  show that many workers are unlikely to speak out about problems in the  workplace if they do not have access to collective voice mechanisms because  they fear reprisal. This is particularly true for non-unionized workers and  those in non-standard work, as well as women. For instance, using survey  data collected in 2005, Lewchuk (2013) concludes that "the precariously  employed were six to seven times more likely to report that raising health and  safety issues would have negative employment consequences".  In the United States, section 7 of the National Labor  Relations Act (NLRA) provides non-supervisory employees, both union and  non-union, with the right to engage in "concerted activity for the purpose of  collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection". As defined by the  U.S. Supreme Court, "mutual aid and protection" includes employees’ efforts to  "improve current terms and conditions of employment or otherwise improve their  lots as employees through channels outside the immediate employee/employer  relationship"Footnote 135 The Act does not limit the manner, time or place in which  employees engage in "concerted activity". While section 7 lists workers’ protected rights, section 8 makes it  unlawful for an employer to "interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in  the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7". The employer’s conduct will be considered as retaliation if  it tends to interfere with the free exercise of employee rights under the NLRA  and "demonstrating motive or actual coercion is therefore not generally  required" (Rogers & Archer, 2016). Sections 7 and 8 were introduced  when the NLRA was enacted in 1935.  Section 7 of the NLRA protects concerted activities by  unionized workers and non-unionized workers, whether they are seeking to  unionize or not (Rogers & Archer, 2016). The spectrum of protected  concerted activities is wide and includes concerted complaints or grievances  presented to employers regarding compensation, benefits or working conditions,  as well as informal discussions between employees about their working  conditions (Fullerton & Millman, 2008). The protected activities must generally be undertaken by two or more  employees seeking to improve their terms or conditions of employment.  Thus, two or more employees addressing their employer about  improving their pay will be exercising their right to protected concerted  activity. However, the  protection can also extend to the actions of one employee, on the condition  that such actions have "the object of initiating or inducing or preparing  for group action or [have] some relation to group action in the interest of the  employees." Footnote 136 Footnote 137 Section 7 will apply when an  employee speaks to his employer on behalf of one or more co-workers about  improving workplace conditions (NLRB, n.d.). Non-union work stoppages and  walkouts are generally protected,Footnote 138 unless they are "unlawful, violent, […] in breach of contract [or]  "irresponsible" because they threaten property damage" (Rogers & Archer,  2016). Section 7 has been interpreted to  extend the "Weingarten" rule (that is, that an employee in a  unionized workplace may request the presence of a union representative at an  investigatory interview which employee reasonably believes might result in  disciplinary action) to cover employees in non-union workplaces.Footnote 139 The use of social media is, to a  certain extent, protected by section 7 as employees have the right to address  work-related issues and share information about pay, benefits, and working  conditions with coworkers on Facebook, YouTube, and other social media. To be  protected, the use of social media must have some relation to group action, or  seek to initiate, induce or prepare for group action, or bring a group  complaint to the attention of management (Neylon O’Brien, 2011; Bemberg, 2018).  For  instance, an employer's decision to  dismiss an employee who posted a comment on Facebook encouraging a terminated  colleague to hire a lawyer and sue the company was over-ruled by the National  Labor Relations Board (NLRB). The Facebook comment was found to be a protected concerted activity  that did not interfere with the employer’s operations.Footnote 140 However, complaints that are made  publicly and are maliciously false will not be protected.Footnote 141 Many employers have social media policies that aim to limit what their  employee may publish. When such policies are found to be overly broad (that is,  when they prohibit lawful activities either explicitly or by being too vague),  the NLRB can order the employer to rescind or modify them.Footnote 142 Protected  concerted activities provide statutory protection against reprisals for  employees wishing to collectively voice concerns. This form of collective voice  is independent from the employer who is required to not interfere. The American  experience suggests that it can be useful in circumstances in which employees  face particularly egregious working conditions and are otherwise unable to  bring about change or improvements.  For  example, in a leading 1962 case (NLRB v. Washington  Aluminum) workers had  complained about the cold temperatures in the facility during the winter. Footnote 143 On a particularly cold day workers arrived to  find the plant completely unheated and seven walked out. The U.S. Supreme Court  upheld the NLRB’s ruling that the company’s termination of these workers was  unlawful. Similarly, in a more recent case a group of restaurant workers who  had been terminated after protesting working conditions appealed to the NLRB  which ordered them reinstated (Greenhouse, 2015). A search on Lexis Advance US conducted in March  2019 yielded 8,993 NLRB cases dealing with section 7, going back as far as  1935. Although this is a small number over a period of more than 80 years, the  number of cases per year has grown substantially in recent years during a time  when private sector unionization has also fallen sharply. Figure 18  plots  the number of cases per year over the 1935 to 2019 period. The number has  increased significantly over the past two decades.   Figure 18: Number of cases before the NLRB  (section 7 NLRA), 1935–2019   Figure 18 - Text version    Dates Number of cases   1935–1939 396   1940–1944 487   1945–1949 24   1950–1954 42   1955–1959 45   1960–1964 102   1965–1969 187   1970–1974 430   1975-1979 916   1980–1984 854   1985–1989 445   1990–1994 443   1995–1999 329   2000–2004 335   2005-2009 753   2010–2014 1806   2015–2019 1565      Source:  Panel analysis of NLRB/Lexis Advance US.    However, it is important to note that the number of cases  related to section 7 is likely to understate the importance of this provision  because of the "threat effect"—employers who are aware of the law and previous  interpretations by the courts will adjust their behaviour in order to be in  compliance and avoid a costly lawsuit.  Unlike some other  mechanisms, the NLRA protection for concerted activity has the advantage of  having been available and used in the United States, a country that shares many  commonalities with Canada’s labour relations system. It is unclear whether the  collective voice achievable with the support of such a protection might develop  into more sustained collective activity, such as achieving union  representation. Nevertheless, adopting a protection for concerted activity  might be helpful for workers in the FRPS with particularly poor working  conditions.  Recommendation 25: The Panel recommends introducing  a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code.  Our recommendation regarding  this protection is two-fold. First, Part III should state that employees have a  right to participate in concerted activities. Second, employees  who have been dismissed,  suspended, laid-off, demoted or otherwise disciplined because they have  exercised their right to concerted activity should be protected against such  reprisals.Footnote 144 Adding a protection for  concerted activity to Part III would also likely enhance workers’  willingness to join participatory initiatives channelled through community  organizations. The Panel views this right as a potentially useful incremental  change to Canada’s labour relations system in the FRPS and one that would bring  the Code more in line with recent Supreme Court interpretations of the  guarantee of freedom of association in section 2(d) of the Canadian Charter of  Rights and Freedoms."
