question: What information must an employer provide to redundant employees in writing, and by when, after giving notice of termination under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Information to Redundant Employees After Termination Notice

### Section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code

According to Section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code, an employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must provide each redundant employee with a statement in writing. This statement must detail, as at the date of the statement, the employee's:

>
"...vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer."

This means the statement must comprehensively cover all financial aspects related to the employee's employment termination.

### Timing of the Statement

The statement must be provided to the redundant employee
"...as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee..." This indicates a strict timeframe for delivering this crucial information. The employer has a responsibility to provide this information promptly, with a deadline of two weeks prior to the termination date.

### Section 213(1) and Cooperation with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission

Furthermore, Section 213(1) highlights the employer's obligation to cooperate with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission (CEI) by providing any information requested by the CEI to assist redundant employees in re-establishing themselves in employment. This underscores the importance of transparency and collaboration with the CEI during the termination process.

question: Can a request for review of a notice of violation be escalated to a higher authority, and under what circumstances?
answer:
## Escalation of Review Requests for Notices of Violation

### General Process for Review

A request for review of a notice of violation can be escalated to a higher authority, specifically the Board, under certain circumstances.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal, in which case the Head shall so inform the applicant and refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of this Part."

This indicates that the Head has the discretion to treat a request for review as an appeal. When this occurs, the request is formally referred to the Board. This essentially elevates the matter from a review process under the Head's authority to an appeal process under the Board's jurisdiction.

### Circumstances for Escalation

The circumstances under which a request for review is escalated are tied to the Head's assessment of the situation.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal..."

This suggests that the decision to escalate is not automatic but depends on the Head's judgment regarding the appropriateness of an appeal. The specific factors considered by the Head are not detailed in this section, but it implies that the Head will consider the nature of the violation, the potential impact, and other relevant factors.

### Alternative Escalation via Appeal (Section 282)

Another avenue for escalation exists, although it is not directly tied to a request for review.
"The Head may, if the Head considers it appropriate in the circumstances, treat the request for review as an appeal of their decision, in which case the Head shall so inform any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance — or, in the case of a compliance order, the employer — and shall refer the request for review to the Board, and the Board shall be considered to have an appeal before it for the purposes of section 251.12."

This section clarifies that the Head can treat a request for review as an appeal of their own decision. This is a distinct process from the initial request for review under section 281.

### Finality of Decision

It is important to note that, subject to the right of appeal under section 251.11, the decision made under subsection (3) is final and conclusive and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court. (CLC-251.101, Section 5) This means that the Board's decision on an appeal is generally final, unless a separate right of appeal exists.

question: In cases where an employee complains about an employer's action related to certain rights, who bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did or did not occur?
answer:
## Burden of Proof in Employee Complaints Regarding Employer Actions

This analysis examines the burden of proof in cases where an employee complains about an employer's actions related to certain rights, drawing from the provided Canada Labour Code sections.

### Section 133 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 133 outlines the process for employees to file complaints with the Board regarding actions taken by employers that contravene Section 147.
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This passage is crucial as it directly addresses the burden of proof in complaints related to the exercise of rights under sections 128 and 129. It states that "the burden of proof is on that party" – meaning the employer – if they allege that the contravention (the employer's action) did not occur. This means that if an employer disputes the employee's claim that they acted in contravention of the Labour Code, the employer must provide evidence to demonstrate that the contravention did not happen.

### Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 6.2 addresses the presumption of employment and the burden of proof in cases where an employer alleges that a person is not their employee.
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

While this section doesn't specifically address employee complaints about employer actions, it establishes a general principle: when an employer disputes the employment status of someone, the employer bears the burden of proving that the person is not an employee. This principle is relevant because an employer might attempt to argue that their actions were not in contravention of the Labour Code by claiming the employee was not an employee.

### Section 133.6 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 133.6 reinforces the burden of proof on the employer when an employee alleges a contravention of Section 147.
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This passage reiterates the principle established in Section 133, emphasizing that if an employer disputes the occurrence of a contravention, they must prove that it did not happen. This ensures that the employer cannot simply deny wrongdoing and avoid accountability.

In summary, when an employee complains about an employer's actions related to certain rights, the burden of proof rests on the employer to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did not occur. This is particularly true when the employee's complaint is based on the exercise of rights under sections 128 and 129 of the Canada Labour Code.

question: Under what conditions can the maximum hours of work for an employee in a week be adjusted or have exceptions?
answer:
## Adjusting and Exceptions to Maximum Hours of Work

### Emergency Work
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit." This indicates that the standard maximum hours can be surpassed during unforeseen circumstances requiring immediate attention. 

### Averaging Hours
"In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks." This outlines a mechanism for adjusting the weekly maximum by averaging hours over a longer period. This is particularly relevant for employees with variable schedules.

### Collective Agreement
"Section 172 (1) An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union." This specifies that if an employer and a trade union agree, the maximum hours can be adjusted for employees covered by a collective agreement, provided the average weekly hours do not exceed 48.

### Modified Work Schedule
"...can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit  for emergency work under an averaging plan under a modified work schedule..." This highlights that modified work schedules can allow for exceeding the standard maximum hours. 

### Exemptions for Certain Classes of Employees
"...drivers in the trucking industry (Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations) employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry (East Coast and Great Lakes Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations, 1985) and the West Coast shipping industry (West Coast Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations) running trades employees in the railway industry (Railway Running-Trades Employees Hours of Work Regulations) the commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry (Broadcasting Industry Commission Salesmen Hours of Work Regulations), and the commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry (Banking Industry Commission-paid Salespeople Hours of Work Regulations)..." This indicates that certain professions are exempt from the standard maximum hours, with specific regulations governing their work hours.

### Student Interns
"If you are a person doing both an unpaid student internship to fulfill the requirements of your educational program and paid employment with the same employer, your total hours of work must not exceed:   10 hours in a day, or 48 hours in a week..." This provides a specific limit for student interns who are also employed.

### Requirements for Creating, Changing or Canceling a Modified Work Schedule
"If you are not covered by a collective agreement:   one employee or a group of employees must approve the modified work schedule:  				 for one employee, the schedule must be approved, in writing, by the affected employee and their employer for a group of employees, the schedule must be approved by at least 70% of the affected employees..." This outlines the process for adjusting work schedules when there is no collective agreement in place.
